desc: magus agent install writes the skills and the AGENTS.md block, and the harness spell for the host prints the hook entry a person merges into the host's config. From then on the host runs the guard's PreToolUse hook before every shell command, file edit and magus MCP call, and only an allowed call runs. The guard reads the job store for the lease the call acts as. The harness sits in the same Go module as the task runner: the guard, the job store and the MCP tools import the graph the targets declare, not a layer above it. Skills, guard verdicts and MCP replies all name commands through internal/hint, so a renamed command cannot leave one of them pointing at nothing.
title: What an agent host gets, and the gate every call crosses

desc: The orchestrator forks job rows into one JSON Lines store and waits on them; it never does groundwork. Each worker is bound to one row: its write paths, its one check, its own checkout, placed by the worktree bootstrap. The integrator merges the finished branches with git merge --no-ff, regenerates once and runs the full checks. The guard reads the row on every write and command. The sandbox narrows a run's writes to the same row, and its filesystem half applies that grant with landlock where the kernel has it. The broker holds the one build budget every checkout on the machine shares.
title: Three roles, one store, and a guard at every boundary

desc: magus-utils reads Go declarations with godecl and the config keys with the config generator. Both hand the emitter a description, and the emitter writes Buzz declarations through buzzgen. The bindings package imports the generated mirrors from its gen directory, so a host module and a Buzz script see the same type. A mirror is generated and committed, never reflected at run time.
title: Go types become Buzz mirrors at build time, never at run time

desc: In a checkout with no ./magus, the guard's raw-tool rule advises exactly one command through, alone on its line: GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2 go run -trimpath ./cmd/magus run go-build --no-cache ., which runs the real go-build target. It regenerates the spell bytecode first and links a stamp of the sources the binary was built from. Every other raw go command, a bare go build included, is refused and served that command; once ./magus exists the rule names ./magus run go-build . instead. The magus on PATH re-execs that ./magus; the stale policy compares its stamp with the checkout, and when a binary can no longer load the tree the same bootstrap is allowed over it, which is the one way back.
title: One go run, then magus builds magus

desc: Session.Exec compiles source in six steps, all in the gopherbuzz root package except the first and the last. The lexer, token.Tokenize, turns the source into tokens; a session given a parse cache keeps them by source text, so a module many sessions import is lexed once. The parser builds an ast.Program. Before the checker sees it, import resolution runs every imported file through this same pipeline and the VM, so their exports are bound when the checker looks names up. The checker reports types.Type mismatches as BZZ diagnostics, and the compiler emits a vm.Chunk, one per function. In the vm package, FoldConsts folds constants and FusePeephole fuses the common local, constant and branch sequences into superinstructions. A session with a bytecode store saves the chunk with every file it was compiled against and, on a later run where all of them still hold the same bytes, hands the saved chunk to the VM without parsing anything.
title: From Buzz source to a chunk

desc: Every Buzz program magus touches goes through the same gopherbuzz pipeline: lex, parse, check, compile, run. Hosts differ only in the modules they register first. The host bindings attach to the magusfile engine at init and provide every magus host module, each through the trampoline generated from its descriptor. The browser playground runs the dry evaluator, which installs only the trampolines marked WASM, pure compute with no filesystem, process or network access, and records host calls instead of running them. Both also install the Buzz stdlib.
title: One pipeline, and the modules each host registers

desc: Session.runChunk makes a VM and calls VM.Run with the chunk and the session's environment. Run reserves the top-level register window and asks jitRun first. With the JIT on, the baseline JIT judges the chunk once and caches the verdict: depths() admits only the numeric subset, locals, constants, arithmetic, comparisons and jumps, and validates every operand, and compileJIT emits amd64 or arm64 code through golang-asm into executable pages. Only the chunk Run was handed can go native; a function it calls runs on the interpreter. There is one native tier and no hotness counter. A value the native code cannot handle deopts to the interpreter at the instruction it stopped on, with the stack depth checked; a chunk the JIT declines, or one with no slot locals, runs on the interpreter from the start. The interpreter's values are NaN-boxed 64-bit words, and heap objects are handles into one table the session releases when it closes.
title: Interpreter first, native code when the chunk allows it

desc: A lookup hashes a target's declared inputs, found by the change set, and asks the local store, then the remote tier over HTTP. A hit restores the outputs by copy-on-write clone where the filesystem has it. A miss runs the target through the spawner, records the run in the journal and, on a trusted branch, signs the entry with the secret and puts it. The job row decides which writes count as the run's own.
title: What a cache lookup reads, and what it writes back

desc: A pull request run reads the signed remote tier and reads and writes a local tier scoped to its own ref. Only a run on the default branch holds the signing key, so only the default branch writes the remote tier. Every read checks the signature and rebuilds the target on an unsigned entry.
title: A pull request reads the shared cache and never writes it

desc: ci.yaml runs on a pull request: the gate sizer in internal/ci picks the shards from the forecast and the volatility score, runs them, and annotates the result. It restores the signed remote cache and writes only a tier scoped to the pull request. cd.yaml runs after a merge to main, renders the site from the profiles CI uploaded and builds the image, and it alone holds the key that writes the shared tier. release.yaml cuts binaries on a tag. Nothing that runs pull-request code holds a secret or a write token.
title: CI validates a change; CD ships what a merge produces

desc: A ci target names its steps in a single needs call, so they are independent and run in parallel. Order comes from edges the steps themselves declare, such as test depending on build. magus enforces none of this list.
title: ci declares steps, not an order

desc: A failing project reaches the annotator contract, which speaks generic verbs to a provider spell; the spell translates them into the CI system's own syntax. Quote prefixes are declared once and applied per line in Go.
title: Vendor syntax lives in the spell, never in the binary

desc: A generated file is committed only when it is a pure function of committed sources, is not already produced by the build, is read by something that never runs the build, and is neither large nor churning.
title: Whether a generated file belongs in the repo

desc: The load reads magus.yaml, the environment and the flags into one set of keys, resolving user and state paths through the xdg directories. A remote source goes through the HTTP client, a daemon address through the endpoint package, and a key that names a ward or a stamp is checked against it. The keys come from one declaration. The generator writes the typed accessors in gen from it, so a flag, a config key and the help text cannot disagree.
title: Every key has one declaration, and every source feeds the same load

desc: A figure in docs/site/diagrams builds its boxes from the knowledge graph's own records, magus\graph().dir, magus\graph().dirs and magus\graph().layer, and draws the imports and declared calls between them. magus/figure lays it out and paints it; diagrams-generate writes the committed light, dark and page copies with a receipt beside each, and the site render inlines the page copy. The server embeds the same module to draw live figures at /api/v1/diagrams, which the console fetches. The job store draws its plan figure through the same module, and each figure's receipt carries a stamp of its boxes and edges, so a stale committed copy is a diff.
title: One library draws every figure, here and in the console

desc: magus doctor runs a list of checks and prints one verdict per check. Each check reads the subsystem it is about: the loaded config, the cache and its remote tier, the spell registry and its overrides, the service audit, the installed agent skills and hooks, and the job, session and trail records. A check reports what is wrong and the command that fixes it; it changes nothing.
title: One check per question, each reading the subsystem it asks about

desc: Almost every CI job builds magus from the commit under test and runs it against that commit's magusfile, so a change can rely on a feature that has not shipped. One audit job instead runs the pinned previous release against the same magusfile; it is advisory, and a failure reports a breaking change rather than blocking the branch.
title: magus builds magus, then runs the last release at it too

desc: internal/dry loads a magusfile or a spell with every host call replaced by a recording stub, so the Buzz runs and nothing outside the process changes. It reads the spell registry and the wards to answer the same way a real run would, uses the generated host mirrors to type the stubs, and hands the recorded graph to the callers: doctor checks a workspace with it, the docs generator runs examples with it and the playground runs a script in a browser.
title: A dry run evaluates a magusfile with the host's effects stubbed

desc: The guard holds the rules and little else of its own. The catalog names every built-in rule and its grade, the workspace supplies the loaded policy, and the config says which rules are denied, advised or off. The interpreter runs the workspace's Buzz rule. To judge a call the guard reads the job store for the lease the call acts as and the session record for what the session already did. It writes each judgement to the trail and names the command to run instead through the hint package.
title: What the guard reads to reach one verdict

desc: The host's PreToolUse hook, wired by magus agent harness install, pipes the event to magus shell. The built-in rules judge it first, reading the job store for the lease the call acts as and the session record for what the session already did; the workspace's magus\guard.command rule sees only what they let through and can only add to the verdict. Each judgement lands in the trail. A deny carries its reason and a next: breadcrumb naming the command to run instead, and the hook renders it into the host's reply.
title: One command judges every call, and says what to run instead

desc: Each supported host has a harness spell under spells/harness: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode, plus the Claude Code mod. A spell knows where its host keeps hook entries and prints the entry a person merges. magus agent install writes the shared half, the embedded skills and the read-only scout agent, through internal/agent. The hook each spell prints runs the guard before every call. The driver in internal/agent/harness runs a host's loop in tests, so a spell's output is proven against a real hook payload.
title: One spell per host writes the hook that reaches the guard

desc: Four layers, top to bottom. The person writes the guard rules, forks the jobs and prompts the agent. The outer harness, magus, judges every call the inner harness makes and answers from the workspace record. The inner harness, the host's agent loop, sends the model its context and executes the tool calls the model proposes. The model only proposes.
title: The model proposes, the harness executes

desc: Top to bottom: the person, the outer harness, the inner harnesses. The person writes the guard rules and forks job rows into the job store. Claude Code and Codex each take a row with magus job exec and return it with magus job exit, and send every call through the guard, which reads the row and the workspace graph and answers with a verdict. The two loops never talk to each other; the records are what they share.
title: Two inner harnesses, one outer harness, shared records

desc: Without the cd charm an image-build loads locally and pushes nothing. With it, the channel decides: the default commit channel adds one immutable tag to one registry, and only stable moves the floating latest tag.
title: What a bare run pushes, and what each channel adds

desc: A target's ctx.readsFiles and ctx.writesFiles globs resolve from its own project's directory. The source walk matches every file a glob names, so the root's **/*.go keys every nested Go file too. An output glob claims a file inside a nested project only when the glob is rooted there; the snapshot, the replay and the drift gate all ask the same rule, and a write that lands there anyway fails the run as MGS3001. A nested project reads the root's tree through a project handle, workspace\file, which also makes the root its upstream. The matched files and the probed tool versions are the key; an input nobody declared never reaches it.
title: An output stops at a nested project; an input does not

desc: The job store keeps one row per job in a JSON Lines file: its goal, checkpoint and write paths, and the leases that release them. Migrations upgrade an old row on read. describe renders the spec an agent reads, the forecast sizes the verifying checks, and the queue types record a landed job. The store reads the session record and the trail to say who held a lease. The guard judges calls against the row, and the sandbox narrows a run's writes to it.
title: A job row is one record, and four packages read it

desc: magus graph build assembles a shard per source: the registry and one per project from the magusfiles, the file adapters for Buzz, docs, directories, citations and CODEOWNERS, a lazy symbol shard per project from a SCIP index, git history and notes. The store fingerprints each shard and rewrites only the ones whose content changed, then merges them into one graph. The CLI and the MCP tools read that graph through the same query, explain, refs and path.
title: Every source writes a shard; every reader asks one graph

desc: Read from deploy/kustomize/overlays/dev without the kustomize binary. One pod, one claim, no token: the default-deny policy shuts every port, and two egress policies open DNS and HTTPS back up.
title: The magus daemon in the dev overlay

desc: The language service answers completion, hover and signature help for Buzz from the lexer's tokens and a manifest of every host module's members. magus serves it to an editor over the language server protocol, and the browser playground runs the same code in WebAssembly beside the dry-run engine, so the two answer the same way.
title: One language service answers the editor and the playground

desc: An orchestrator checkpoints the revision through vcs, partitions the work by write set and forks one job row per unit into the job store: goal, checkpoint, write paths. describe prints the row a worker reads. The guard reads the row on every call. Holders release paths as soon as they are done, so the plan shrinks while it runs, and the Jobs view renders the rows for whoever is watching. The change set verifies each job by diffing since that job's checkpoint against what it claimed. magus records and answers; it enforces none of it beyond the guard.
title: A declared plan, released early, verified by diff

desc: The risk tiers magus proves, lowest first. The person types --tolerance when issuing a mandate, at most this repository's ceiling, mechanical. An unsettled job whose change proves at or below it is integrated with no one present; one above it is held for review. A settled job is integrated through its gates at any tier.
title: A mandate raises the bar at its tolerance

desc: Four rows: the person decides, the plan, the mandate and each grant write the decision down, the guard judges every call against them, and the root and its workers do the work. Every call either one makes goes to the guard, whose verdict is allow, deny or advise. The root forks jobs and spawns workers; a worker's hand-back wakes the root. What a job did ends integrated or held for review, and the report hands that back to the person.
title: The person decides; the guard enforces what they wrote down

desc: For a conflicted file the queue asks the classifier which class the edit is and settles only a low-risk one, kicking code back, then gates the projects the magus SDK says the change reaches, or every project when that set is no proof.
title: What a candidate's risk makes the queue run

desc: queue-intent runs when a pull request asks to merge and records the intent. queue plans the batch with the engine, asks the forge provider for the changes and runs the repository's gate script on the candidate. queue-apply merges the candidate the gate passed and reports the rest. The workflows are YAML; the decisions are the engine's, so the same queue runs from any forge that has a provider.
title: Three workflows drive the queue, and one script gates it

desc: Built files and an optional digest-pinned base reach libs/image through the image host module. libs/image assembles each layer, stages one layout per platform, combines the layouts into an index and attaches referrers, cloning files copy-on-write where the filesystem has it. libs/oci is the registry client: it resolves the base by digest and publishes the result.
title: OCI assembly: files in, a layout out, a registry after

desc: magus accepts a workspace URL, a workspace-relative path, a dot-relative path or the bare root alias, and parses them all to one project reference. Human output prints the short path; machine output prints the workspace URL.
title: Four spellings in, one reference out

desc: A spell reaches the sandbox from two sides: the interpreter runs its Buzz in process, and the spawner starts its tool. The sandbox builds one grant. The filesystem half names the readable and writable paths and applies them with landlock where the kernel has it. The environment half rebuilds the child's variables from an allowlist. A job's write paths narrow the writes, a refusal lands in the trail, and the journal keeps the denial.
title: What a spell may touch while it runs

desc: Agents and the console reach /mcp, the /api/v1 read views, the review and plan routes and the typed Connect services through the DNS-rebind, bearer-token and CORS guard. POST /api/v1/diff/session carries the human half of a paired review and POST /api/v1/share opens the LAN listener; both are loopback only. The health endpoints answer probes directly, with no authentication.
title: The HTTP routes, and the one route without a guard

desc: File changes reach the watchers, which tell the workspace registry what to invalidate. A magus run queues a coalesced graph-build job on the server, which rebuilds the knowledge graph and writes it back into the registry, the server's single warm copy.
title: What keeps the warm workspace current

desc: Sharing from the dashboard posts to a loopback-only endpoint, which mints a time-boxed read-only token and opens an ephemeral LAN listener. The listener serves four JSON read routes and the read Connect services, and nothing else. Every other handler in the console's handler layer stays loopback only: the graph, the diff routes, the derived plan, the job store, /mcp and job control.
title: The only listener a second machine can reach

desc: The magus CLI dispatches over a private unix domain socket into the concurrency pool, the workspace registry and the run registry; shared services go to the broker. Sharing a graph spawns a separate short-lived loopback server.
title: How a local command reaches the server

desc: A service op names a long-running process. internal/service starts it through the spawner and keeps the record of the run, keyed by an identity that survives a restart. The ward checks the op's argv against its declared kind before it runs, the audit finds a recorded service whose op is gone, and the host bindings and doctor read the same identity. The identity package holds the key and nothing else, so every reader agrees on what one service is.
title: A service op is one long-running process with one identity

desc: Each agent host session gets one record: who started it, its checkout and what it did. The guard appends to it on every call, and the journal underneath keeps the append-only lines. The trail reads the record to say which session made a change, the agent install reads it to rehydrate a session that lost its history, and the console's attention and viewer handlers show it to the person watching.
title: A session record is written by the hook and read by four others

desc: Each language has an indexer behind one contract. The Go indexer wraps a Go analyzer, the Buzz indexer parses with scipbuzz, and the shell indexer reads scripts. The contract fixes the result as one SCIP file per project. The bindings and the spell host call the indexers when a project's sources change, and the knowledge graph opens that file one project at a time instead of loading every symbol.
title: A SCIP indexer per language writes the file the graph reads lazily

desc: magus refuses a ci run when no project in scope declares ci. Every other step, and the order between them, is the convention this workspace follows so each verb means the same thing in every project.
title: Only ci is required; the rest is an order

desc: types holds the records every other package passes around: targets, runs, findings, jobs. Its enums sit in types/enum, and the diagnostic codes come from libs/diagnostics. The daemon, diff, event, trail and image groups split off the records that only some callers need, and each imports the base and the enums, never the other way. Encoding lives on the type through the shared JSON package, so no reader splits lines itself.
title: The shared records sit at the bottom, and the groups lean on them

desc: The vcs package names the revision, the branch, the dirty digest and the changed files for whichever backend the checkout uses, so no other package runs a VCS command. Job leases and the cache key read the revision, the session and trail records stamp it, and the landing code reads the branch and the merge base. The package reads files through internal/file, identifies itself with the build stamp and keeps its state in the XDG directories.
title: One VCS interface answers git, Mercurial, Sapling and Jujutsu

desc: A failing target that opted in is retried once while its history is too thin to judge, when the diff did not touch its project, or when its measured volatility is above the threshold. A retry that passes is recorded as volatile and the run continues; anything else is a suspected regression.
title: When a failure is retried, and when it is believed

desc: Discovery walks the tree from the root marker and registers one project per magusfile: the root's is project ., each nested one declares its own. Every magusfile is evaluated: its exported functions are its targets and magus\project layers policy on. A static read of each target body recovers ctx.readsFiles, ctx.writesFiles and cross-project ctx.needs as literals. The project model that results is what the cache keys, what describe answers from, and what a command resolves its project against from the current directory.
title: A target exists because a magusfile exported it
